SIGNAL

SATYA NADELLA IS AGI-PILLED NOW

What happened: At a roundtable after his Ignite keynote https://every.to/emails/click/136f006095268802530f927779a5f4d55a493840c0f1f77c950761a77b64df9e/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiTWljcm9zb2Z0J3MgQ0VPIFdhbnRzIEV2ZXJ5IENvbXBhbnkgdG8gT3duIEl0cyBPd24gTW9kZWwiLCJwb3N0X2lkIjo0NjIzLCJwb3N0X3R5cGUiOiJwb3N0IiwidXJsIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cueW91dHViZS5jb20vd2F0Y2g_?ev_audience=free on Tuesday, Nadella said he is “AGI pilled,” though not in the usual sense of betting on superintelligence. What matters to him is how the political economy will be organized around a model with “no limits”—one that could become a health care or financial services company, or even “take over the government.”

Why it matters: Microsoft is making its case against Anthropic taking over everything. Asked whether Anthropic can still be caught once its models start improving themselves, Nadella said a world that runs on one firm structurally won’t happen because the world will demand more than one firm. He made the same point in his keynote: Intelligence needs to be broadly distributed for multiple firms to thrive, which means there should be “as many models as firms.”

What it means: Microsoft is rebuilding its model business, its product, and its own teams around that bet.

 * Customers make models their own. Nadella says he’s trying to convert the model business into a “database business.” Microsoft will let enterprise customers license its MAI model weights https://every.?ev_audience=free, run them in their own Azure environments, fine-tune them on proprietary data, and decide when to upgrade. AT&T has already tried it: Its custom MAI model outperformed Sol 6.1 on standard 5G network tasks at one-fiftieth of the cost, according to Microsoft. Monologue https://every.?ev_audience=free, Every’s dictation app, runs on a similar idea: Its two-person team replaced a roughly 1-trillion-parameter model with one they fine-tuned themselves https://every.?ev_audience=free, and it’s faster and far cheaper.
 * Copilot goes multiplayer. As head of evals Mike Taylor https://every.?ev_audience=free wrote in August https://every.?ev_audience=free, Claude Code’s bottom-up surge eventually pushed Microsoft to break its exclusivity with OpenAI and bring Claude into Copilot. Now, Microsoft’s latest moves, like the launch of Autopilot https://every.?ev_audience=free (Microsoft’s answer to products like Dots and Duet), suggest the company has to build a better Claude desktop before Claude builds a better Office suite. Copilot used to be a sidebar inside Office. Now the full Office apps run inside Copilot, and Copilot Workspaces https://every.?ev_audience=free lets people and their agents collaborate using shared context.
 * The firm changes, too. Nadella says Microsoft’s ideal team stack now includes full-stack builders, infrastructure people, and scientists, and former team leads are becoming individual contributors who manage agents. (As Ryan Sloan https://every.?ev_audience=free reported for us in September https://every.?ev_audience=free, Microsoft has put Copilot’s agents on the org chart.) Nadella says those contributors will get a token budget, and yes, their pay should go up as an incentive. Most importantly, he stressed that everyone (including him) needs to relearn how work happens from first principles. “We turn our two hundred thousand people into a scale benefit, but it has to transform and work like any AI native startup.”

‘THE EVERY PODCAST’: NOTION’S CEO ON WHEN AND WHEN NOT TO BUILD YOUR OWN TOOLS


https://every.?ev_audience=free

Ivan Zhao started Notion 13 years ago to give nontechnical people the building blocks to make software without learning to code. AI has made that easier, and Zhao is still a believer. At Thesis: 2027, he told Dan where he draws the line.

On this week’s episode of The Every Podcast, we’re sharing Zhao’s conversation with Dan on which tools are worth building yourself, why your data matters more than the interface, and how to keep track of what your agents build.

Watch on X https://every.?ev_audience=free or YouTube https://every.?ev_audience=free, or listen on Spotify https://every.?ev_audience=free or Apple Podcasts https://every.?ev_audience=free. You can also read the transcript https://every.?ev_audience=free.

Here are the highlights:

 * Build the tools you want to tinker with. Zhao sorts software into three buckets. Build the tools you use every day and want to customize. Buy the ones you would rather someone else got right, along with the systems your company depends on for security and would struggle to maintain. Notion’s business depends on the last two. Zhao compares it to eating out: “Yes, you can cook yourself, but oftentimes you like to go to a restaurant as well.”
 * Organize the data your agents need. Agents can write a workflow or spin up an interface, but they still need access to what your team knows. That’s why Zhao sees Notion as a keeper of company data. Teams can give their preferred agents access while keeping controls on what people can see and edit. He also thinks well-organized data could save money by helping agents spend fewer tokens piecing together what the company already knows.
 * Keep track of what your agents build. Give agents a sizable codebase, Zhao says, and within a week “you sort of don’t understand what’s going on.” He wants toolmakers to give people better ways to see how the pieces fit together. At Notion, one answer turned out to be the dreaded kanban board. The thing “everybody hate[s]” gave the team a way to see what its agents were working on.

This is a must-watch for anyone wanting to build with AI without losing track of what they’ve built.
